ONE MORE ORBIT: art bible

Three directions for a mature, hand-made look, each shown as the same four pictures: the hero, the boss, the galaxy map, and a moment of play during a drop. Nothing in the game has changed. Pick one (or a mix) and I apply it everywhere.

What these pictures are, plainly. I drew all twelve in code, on a canvas, with tools I wrote for the job: paper grain and fibres, uneven washes, brush passes, a burin's wavering hatching, gold leaf with flecks, halftone dots, plates out of register. No image generator and no stock art. The upside is that everything you see here can be drawn by the game itself. The limit is real too: code can make texture, light and good shapes, but it is not a painter's hand. Section 6 is the brief for a human illustrator, for the key art where that hand matters most.

1. What changes in every direction

  • No faces. Eko is a flame with a seed of light in it, a wisp that follows a beat behind, and the ring he wears. He speaks through how he leans, flares and trails. The Hush has no mouth and no cute eye: it is a mass that takes light, with one lidded sliver that looks back.
  • Light has a source. On the map every planet is lit from the Lantern, so its lit side always faces the lighthouse. In play, Eko and the planet are the lights. The Hush gives none.
  • Texture on everything, sparkles on nothing. Stars are dabs, points or dots, gathered into bands. The four-point sparkle is gone.
  • One language from map to play. The same paper, the same line or brush, the same type. The planet you chose on the map is the one at the centre of your rings.
  • Play stays clean. Rings, marks, hazards and Eko are drawn last, on a calm ground, with a dark edge under them. White is still only ever "tap here". Style lives behind, in the effects and in the small shapes.
  • Each planet has its own palette, tied to its song (listed per direction below).

2. Direction A: Afterglow

Gouache and watercolour at dusk. Deep air, soft volumes of light, silhouettes, paper grain.

Mood, never a modelThe wide quiet of Journey, the watercolour of Gris, the dusk of Alto's Odyssey; gouache landscape studies; stage lighting.
PaletteEvery scene is one dusk: a sky graded from a deep cool to a single warm, and Eko is always the warmest thing in it. Emberwick: ember and plum. Cirra: rose and pale gold cloud. Glassmere: ice blue and slate. Verdance: deep teal and leaf light. The Hollow: violet grey with no warm at all, until the end.
BrushWet washes that pool at their edges, long dry strokes laid across the skies, soft blooms where paint ran, paper tooth and fibres over everything. No ruled edge anywhere.
LightVolumes, not lines. Beams are soft cones; each planet has a rim on the Lantern's side and falls into shade; haze sits where land meets sky; Eko's glow falls off across the ground.
TypeA soft old-style serif, italic for names (proposed: Fraunces or Cormorant). Planet names and the logo lettered with a brush.
From map to playA planet's sky on the map is the backdrop of its level, and the ridges at the bottom of the play field are its horizon. The rings are chalk on the painting.
MotionRidges and haze slide at different speeds. The wisp follows on a spring and overshoots. Light swells through the build and bursts in wide strokes at the drop. The Hush's curtains sway on a long, uneven period.
Eko and the HushEko: a small flame in a very large place. The Hush: a mountain of hanging fog with an eclipse in its hood, mostly lidded; the songs it took hang from threads in jars.

3. Direction B: Star Atlas

Ink on dark paper: a burin's line, hatching for shade, gold leaf for whatever gives light, and the music drawn as constellations.

Mood, never a modelCelestial atlases and copperplate star charts of the 1600s and 1700s, alchemical diagrams, gilded manuscripts, brass instruments.
PaletteDark paper, parchment ink, and leaf. Colour is rationed: gold only where something gives light, vermilion only for danger. Each planet adds one wash under the line and its own metal. Emberwick: sepia and red gold. Cirra: rose grey and pale gold. Glassmere: blue black and silver leaf. Verdance: verdigris and brass. The Hollow: bare ink, no leaf until it is beaten.
LineOne fine line of even weight. Shade is hatching that follows the form, crossed in the deep. Lines waver and break. Leaf has flecks and gaps. Plate borders, plate numbers, and small notes in a clerk's italic.
LightBy how close the lines are, never by gradient. The lit side is left open with leaf on its limb, the far side is hatched. The Lantern's beam is a fan of ruled gold lines.
TypeA high-contrast engraved serif in spaced small capitals, italic for notes (proposed: Cormorant SC with IM Fell English). Logo and planet names as engraved lettering.
From map to playThe map is a plate of the atlas. Play is the same plate seen close: rings are graduated circles, gold notes are stars joined into a constellation, a shard branch is a small constellation to complete, and the drop is a burst of ruled lines and thrown leaf.
MotionLines draw themselves in like a pen stroke, they do not fade in. Leaf catches the light as things turn. The Hush's cloth sags and swings, and the stars near it go hollow one by one.
Eko and the HushEko: an engraved flame shaded along its own rise, with a seed of gold and a ring like an armillary's. The Hush: an eclipse, a black disc with cloth hanging off it in every direction, one seam sewn shut and a hair of light under it.

4. Direction C: Night Press

A screen-printed poster: one flood of midnight ink on cream stock, two spot inks per planet, halftone for every gradient, nothing quite in register.

Mood, never a modelScreen-printed gig and travel posters, risograph zines, mid-century record sleeves, cut-paper collage.
PaletteMidnight ink on cream paper, plus two inks per planet; where they overlap they make the third colour. Emberwick: orange and yellow. Cirra: pink and cream. Glassmere: aqua and cream. Verdance: green and yellow. The Hollow: solid black and one violet.
TextureHalftone dots for every gradient, grain in every flat, the second ink always a little off, registration marks and colour bars in the margin, bare paper for the brightest things.
LightFlat shapes with a halftone shade on the side away from the Lantern. Beams are wedges of dots that thin with distance.
TypeHeavy condensed capitals, large and tight, with small spaced labels (proposed: a condensed grotesque such as Archivo for headlines; Unbounded could stay for numerals). The logo cut as a poster wordmark.
From map to playThe map is a poster; a level is the same poster moving. Rings are thick strokes of paper colour, and the drop splits the sheet into turning wedges of two inks.
MotionThings land and settle, as if stamped. Eko leaves echoes behind him like stacked prints. On each beat a plate lands slightly off and slides into register.
Eko and the HushEko: two leaves of flame, one printed over the other, with a seed of bare paper. The Hush: the top of the sheet printed solid black and quilted, with one slit left unprinted.

5. Side by side, and what I would pick

A. AfterglowB. Star AtlasC. Night Press
Feels likeQuiet, wide, a little sadOld, learned, mysteriousLoud, confident, modern
Hand-made by code aloneHardest: paint is the thing code fakes worstBest: line, hatching and leaf are convincingGood: grain and misregistration carry it
Readability in playGood, needs the dark band under the courseBest: the page is already dark and quietVery good: thick marks, flat grounds
Ties to the musicLight swells with the songNotes are stars, phrases are constellationsEach beat is a plate printed over the last
RiskCan slide into soft gradientsCan feel cold without colour washesCan slide back to flat vector if texture is thin
Needs an illustratorYes, for it to be truly paintedHelpful, not requiredHelpful for the logo and posters

My recommendation: B, Star Atlas, with one thing borrowed from A: a single wash of colour per planet under the engraving, and A's swelling light for the drop. It is the most distinctive of the three, it turns the game's own idea (music you read on a ring) into its look, it is the easiest to keep readable, and it is the one I can make feel hand-made without a painter. A is the most moving but depends most on a human hand. C is the boldest but the closest to where we are now.

6. Brief for an illustrator (draft, one page)

Written so you can hand it over as it is. The first paragraph gets the chosen direction's text once you pick.

ONE MORE ORBIT: key art brief

The game. A one-button rhythm game. A small flame-spirit, Eko, rides rings round planets in time with the music to bring their songs home from the Hush, a vast silence that has taken them. Mood: mature, mysterious, hand-made. No cute faces; character comes from silhouette, light and movement.

Direction. [the chosen direction's paragraph: medium, palette rule, how light works, with the four stills attached as reference for mood only, not for copying]

What we need

AssetMaster sizeSeparate layers (for animation in the game)
Eko, the hero2048 × 2048Flame in three depths (outer, middle, seed); wisp in 4 to 6 segments; ring back half and front half; glow on its own layer. One extra attachment each for his four other forms (Meteor, Satellite, Pulsar, Comet). Must read as a silhouette at 24 px.
Marlow, the keeper (captured)2048 × 2048Body, each wing, antennae, hand lantern and its glow, the jar's glass in front and behind.
The Hush, the boss4096 × 2304Far fog, the mass, 8 to 12 strips of hanging cloth (they sway), the hood and the lid over its light as its own layer (it opens), each thread and jar on its own. Three states: it wakes, it reaches, it unravels.
Five planets1024 × 1024 eachThe globe, its air or glow, a silent state (song taken) and a night side. Plus one backdrop each at 2560 × 1440 in three depths (far, middle, near) with transparency.
LogovectorHand-lettered. Stacked and one-line versions, one-colour version.
App icon1024 × 1024No transparency, subject inside the middle 80%. A simplified 32 px version.

Files

  • Layered source (PSD or Procreate) and every layer exported as PNG with transparency, sRGB.
  • Glows and light on their own layers, never baked into the art (the game adds them).
  • One light direction throughout: on the map, from the lighthouse at the centre; on characters, from Eko.
  • Texture fine enough that paper grain is about one pixel at the sizes above.

Rules

  • Fully original. Nothing that resembles an existing game's characters, and no generated imagery in the source files.
  • Full rights assigned to the project; credit in the game.
  • Three rounds: silhouette sketches (three options per character), a colour key, finals.

How the files go into the game

  • They live in the project under public/art/, packed to WebP with a PNG fallback, about 6 MB in total.
  • The game's canvas draws each layer as a sprite and moves the layers itself: the wisp follows on a spring, the cloth sways, the lid opens with the boss's phases, backdrops slide at different speeds as the camera moves.
  • Menus and story cards use the same files, so map, cards and play are one world. Rings, marks and hazards stay drawn by the game, on top, for clarity.

7. After you pick

  • I finish the art bible for that direction: the full palette for each planet, Eko's five forms, Marlow, the three boss phases, type and motion rules.
  • Then I redraw the characters, the map, the story cards, the menus and the play field in it, and send before and after screenshots on phone and desktop.
  • Typefaces: the stills use stand-in fonts from this Mac. I name a proposed open-licence face for each direction below; I will check each licence before bundling anything, and ask you first, as nothing here should cost money.
